answer.evidence: The top band at rows 3-9 is speckled stone and ends in a lighter front-edge line at row 10. Two dark eave-shadow rows (11-12) follow, and the brick lintel and stone piers sit below as the front face. The stairs at the bottom repeat the pattern: a light edge line at row 64, tread rows 65-68, then dark riser rows 69-71 and a second tread/riser pair. The dark edge columns are the gate's own piers and are not receding side faces. The silhouette is symmetric and front-facing. styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a dark stone gate with a glowing doorway. It has some stone block shading and speckle on the lintel, but the main material ramps hold about 3-4 steps, against 5-6 on the references' roofs and walls. Visible tones per tile are 7, against 10-12 for the references, which is lower but not far off. Near-flat coverage is 13%, against 0% for both references, so there are some flat areas, mainly the dark doorway interior and the stone pillars. Dark edge pixels are 52% neutral, against 7-9% for the references. The outline is therefore partly near-black and partly tinted, which reads as mixed and leans toward the sticker look. Stones are shaded as blocks, but the shading is less varied than the reference tile scallops and plaster speckle. The piece is cleanly drawn and coherent, but a careful artist would see it as flatter and thinner than the references, so it fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone gate with a lintel, pillars, a dark doorway with a red glow, and steps. It has some stone-block shading and speckle on the lintel. It is clean and coherent, but it is flatter and more outlined than Beodeul, and I would not accept it next to the references without it looking thinner. When in doubt, fail.
